sections.text:
Action-chunking vision-language-action (VLA) models predict sequences of future robot actions. Under fixed-horizon execution, the robot executes a fixedlength prefix of each predicted chunk before invoking the policy again, leaving the remaining predictions unused. For a given number of executed actions, short execution horizons require more policy calls.

Extending the execution horizon amortizes policy inference cost over more actions. However, uniformly applying long horizons across episodes can limit opportunities for precise corrections.

To address this limitation, we propose PICES (Perturbation-Informed Chunk and Execution Horizon Selection), a training-free method that jointly selects an action chunk and the number of actions executed before the next policy call.

Within a single policy call, the action expert generates a batch of action chunks from multiple initial noise samples and their locally perturbed counterparts, using the same conditioning features across all samples.

PICES exploits differences between corresponding actions in each nominal chunk and its counterpart to determine candidate-specific execution horizons and select a nominal chunk for execution.

Experiments on simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that PICES achieves speedup by up to 2.3x in wall-clock policy inference time on Jetson Orin and Thor relative to fixed horizon baselines while improving the success rate.

items.title: Accelerating VLA Inference with Perturbation Informed Execution

sections.text:
This work introduces Spatial Annotations from Robot Demonstrations with Reliability Calibration (SPARC), a risk-aware framework that automatically labels robot demonstrations with structured spatial annotations and assigns each annotation a reliability score.

Structured spatial annotations, such as bounding boxes, object trajectories, and manipulation phase labels, benefit a broad range of robotics applications from training grounded robot policies and embodied foundation models to motion planning and hierarchical task composition.

Existing automated pipelines generate such annotations at scale but provide no reliable quality signal: detector confidence is poorly calibrated for annotation correctness, forcing a choice between accepting noisy labels or discarding useful samples.

In contrast to existing automated pipelines, SPARC leverages the spatio-temporal structure inherent to robot tasks to generate a reliability signal, reducing noisy labels and retaining more useful samples.

We further introduce Interaction-Aware Bench (IA-Bench), a benchmark that measures model accuracy in grounding the locations of interacted objects in robot demonstrations.

On 1.7k human-annotated demonstrations spanning diverse embodiments and scenarios, SPARC significantly outperforms detection-only baselines in localization accuracy while retaining three times more samples at high-precision operating points.

Our experiments demonstrate that models finetuned on our annotations achieve state-of-the-art results on object-grounding and pointing benchmarks among similarly sized models, while remaining competitive on broader spatial-reasoning suites without manually verified or annotated training data.

Furthermore, policies trained on SPARC-generated annotations outperform baselines in cluttered, visually ambiguous real-world scenes. Code, data, and models are available at intuitive-robots.github.io/sparc-labeling.

items.title: SPARC: Reliable Spatial Annotations from Robot Demonstrations at Scale

sections.text:
Zero-shot object navigation (ZSON) requires robots to find target objects in unseen environments without task-specific fine-tuning or pre-built maps, a key capability for general-purpose service robots.

Yet methods that perform well in simulation often degrade in cluttered real-world scenes with severe occlusion and latent hazards, where large unseen regions make single-scene inference brittle and unsafe. We propose Schr\"odinger's Navigator, a belief-aware framework that reasons at inference time over multiple trajectory-conditioned imagined 3D futures.

Given candidate paths, a trajectory-conditioned 3D world model predicts hypothetical observations and maintains a superposition of plausible scene realizations rather than committing to one map.

An adaptive occluder-aware sampler directs imagination to uncertainty-critical regions, while a Future-Aware Value Map (FAVM) aggregates imagined futures for robust, proactive action selection.

Experiments in simulation and on a physical Go2 quadruped show that Schr\"odinger's Navigator outperforms strong ZSON baselines, improving hidden-target discovery and risk-aware waypoint selection in occlusion-heavy navigation scenarios.

These results highlight imagined 3D futures as a scalable and generalizable strategy for zero-shot navigation in uncertain real-world environments.

items.title: Schr\"odinger's Navigator: Imagining an Ensemble of Futures for Zero-Shot Object Navigation

sections.text:
We study multi-robot motion planning in a polygonal environment with polygonal robots. The setting of the problem consists of a polygonal domain $\mathcal{W}$ with $n$ vertices and $k$ robots $R_1,\dots,R_k$ translating in $\mathcal{W}$ each of which is represented by a polygon of constant complexity.

Given a source configuration $\mathbf{s}$ and a target configuration $\mathbf{t}$ of the robots in $\mathcal{W}$, the goal of the problem is to find a collision-free motion plan from $\mathbf{s}$ to $\mathbf{t}$ that is shortest with respect to some cost function.

We present the first fully polynomial-time approximation schemes (FPTAS) for motion planning with any fixed number $k$ of robots, under the min-sum objective, the min-max objective, and the min-makespan objective.

Here, the min-sum variant aims to minimize the total traveling distance of all robots, the min-max variant aims to minimize the maximum traveling distance of a single robot, and the min-makespan variant aims to minimize the total time cost under the assumption that all robots move with a maximum speed $1$.

The algorithm directly generalizes to the problem in any fixed dimension $d$, with a polytope environment and polytope robots.

Our result settles an open question of Agarwal, Halperin, Sharir, Steiger [SODA'24] and Agarwal, Holmgren, Steiger [SODA'26], who gave an FPTAS for $k=2$ unit-square robots and a bicriteria-approximation algorithm for a fixed number $k$ of unit-square or unit-disk robots, respectively. Compared to the previous results, our algorithm is substantially simpler.

items.title: FPTAS for Polygonal Multi-Robot Motion Planning

sections.text:
Pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs) often fail midway through unseen long-horizon tasks.

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a remedy, but embodied RSI methods either refine the harness around a frozen executor and so cannot add a missing motion, or train the executor on persistent failures without asking whether a failure lies in how the executor is called or in what it can do.

We ask when a self-improving embodied system should change the weights of its executor, and propose AdaRSI, an on-demand RSI framework for embodied agents.

A coding agent first improves its skills and harness, then attributes persistent failures by retrying failing sub-steps from saved states, and fine-tunes only the sub-steps that remain unreliable, with demonstrations it collects itself and experience carried over from earlier tasks.

On all 50 target tasks of RoboCasa365, with GR00T N1.5 as the executor and no human demonstrations, AdaRSI improves the VLA on all three suites and raises its success on unseen composite tasks from 4.6% to 13.8%.

Compared with fine-tuning every sub-step, it reaches slightly higher success while using only 28% of the GPU time and 22% of the self-collected demonstrations, and fine-tuning without a harness trains more yet gains far less.

items.title: AdaRSI: On-Demand Recursive Self-Improvement for Embodied Agents

sections.text:
Learning a collective policy for state-based Cartesian manipulation across diverse robotic embodiments presents a fundamental challenge due to embodiment-dependent transition dynamics.

Collective learning aggregates multi-robot experience to discover shared task structure, yet naive aggregation can average incompatible action modes when different embodiments realize the same Cartesian command through different transition behavior. This leads to strategy ambiguity and performance collapse on dynamically outlying embodiments.

To address this, we propose PACE, a two-stage collective learning framework that separates shared task-space intent from embodiment-dependent transition dynamics. The first stage employs a representation layer pre-trained on offline trajectories to extract task-level context from collective data.

The second stage introduces a decision layer equipped with a predictive dynamics adapter. By forcing the latent state to predict future transitions, this adapter acts as a latent regularizer that grounds the policy in the transition behavior of the executing robot while preserving real-time inference without online planning.

Evaluations across simulated embodiments demonstrate that our method prevents performance collapse on distinct robots. It achieves over 93\% overall success and 89\% on dynamically out-of-distribution zero-shot simulated robots, outperforming the Transformer behavior cloning (82\%) and diffusion policy baselines (66\%).

Physical KUKA deployment further validates the feasibility of the full state-based pipeline under zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.

items.title: Collective Learning for Unified Robotic Manipulation via Predictive Dynamics Adaptation

sections.text:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have recently achieved remarkable progress by leveraging large-scale robot datasets and foundation models for general-purpose robot manipulation. However, their ability to rapidly adapt to novel manipulation tasks beyond the training distribution remains limited.

Existing approaches often require task-specific robot demonstrations and additional training, which are labor- and compute-intensive, limiting the scalability of VLA adaptation to open-world scenarios.

To reduce this dependence on target-task robot data, we propose CapPro, a framework that enables a VLA policy to adapt to previously unseen manipulation tasks using only a single human demonstration video. CapPro consists of two components.

First, a phase-aware human video representation module constructs a compact video representation through learned visual token selection and learns task-relevant query representations under phase-caption supervision.

Second, a video-conditioned adaptation module jointly incorporates the compact video and query-derived representations into the action-conditioning context of the pretrained VLA policy. % This design introduces task-specific guidance while largely preserving the original VLA action-generation backbone.

In this way, the human demonstration provides task-specific execution guidance rather than an embodiment-aligned trajectory to imitate, without requiring target-task robot demonstrations or target-task fine-tuning.

Experiments across source and unseen target tasks show that CapPro improves average performance across unseen target groups while maintaining comparable performance on the source tasks. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of human-video guidance for cross-task VLA adaptation.

summary.en: The paper introduces CapPro, which adapts a vision-language-action policy to unseen manipulation tasks from a single human demonstration video. It builds a compact video representation and task-relevant queries using visual token selection and phase-caption supervision, then incorporates them into the pretrained policy’s action-conditioning context. The video provides task-specific execution guidance without target-task robot demonstrations or fine-tuning. Experiments on source and unseen target tasks report improved average performance across unseen target groups while maintaining comparable source-task performance.
summary.zh: 论文提出 CapPro，使视觉-语言-动作（VLA）策略仅凭一段人类示范视频适应未见过的操作任务。方法先通过视觉词元选择和阶段字幕监督构建紧凑视频表示及任务相关查询，再将其与预训练 VLA 策略的动作条件上下文结合。人类视频提供任务执行指引，无需目标任务的机器人示范或微调。源任务和未见目标任务实验显示，CapPro 提升了未见目标任务组的平均表现，同时在源任务上保持相近表现。

items.title: One-shot Human Video-Guided Adaptation for Vision-Language-Action Models

sections.text:
This paper rethinks steady-hand robotic manipulation by using a weakly supervised framework that fuses calibration-aware perception with admittance control.

Unlike conventional automation that relies on labor-intensive 2D labeling, our framework leverages reusable warm-up trajectories to extract implicit spatial information, thereby achieving calibration-aware, depth-resolved perception without the need for external fiducials or frame-by-frame manual depth annotation.

By explicitly characterizing residuals from observation and calibration models, the system establishes a task-space error budget from recorded warm-ups.

Under the evaluated laboratory conditions, the recorded trajectories yielded an empirical lateral error level of approximately 49{\mu}m and a conservative axial error estimate of approximately 291 {\mu}m during large in-plane moves.

In a within-subject user study (N=8), the learned agent reduces overall NASA-TLX workload by 77.1% relative to the simple steady-hand assistance baseline.

Together, these results demonstrate successful closed-loop micromanipulation and reduced subjective workload under the evaluated laboratory conditions, without external fiducials or frame-by-frame manual depth annotation, supporting the proposed approach as a framework for microscope-guided robotic assistance.

summary.en: The paper presents a weakly supervised framework for microscope-guided robot assistance, combining calibration-aware perception with admittance control. Reusable warm-up trajectories provide implicit spatial information for depth-resolved perception without external fiducials or frame-by-frame manual depth annotation. The system uses observation and calibration residuals to establish a task-space error budget. Under the evaluated laboratory conditions, trajectories yielded an empirical lateral error of about 49 μm and a conservative axial error estimate of about 291 μm during large in-plane moves. In a within-subject study of eight participants, the agent reduced overall NASA-TLX workload by 77.1% versus a simple steady-hand baseline.
summary.zh: 论文提出一种用于显微镜下机器人辅助操作的弱监督框架，结合校准感知与导纳控制。框架从可复用的预热轨迹中提取隐含空间信息，以实现具备深度分辨能力的感知，无需外部标记或逐帧人工深度标注；并依据观测和校准模型残差建立任务空间误差预算。在所评估的实验室条件下，轨迹测得的横向误差约为49微米，大幅平面内移动时的保守轴向误差估计约为291微米。8名参与者的组内研究显示，相较简单的稳手辅助基线，学习型代理使总体 NASA-TLX 工作负荷降低77.1%。

items.title: Learning From a Steady Hand: A Weakly Supervised Agent for Robot Assistance under Microscopy

sections.text:
Recent world-action models (WAMs) show that co-training policies with future prediction can provide physical priors for action generation. Building on the future-prediction ability of video models, many WAMs generate future videos and recover actions with inverse-dynamics models, or use these predicted videos as goal conditions for action generation.

In both cases, the world model is trained mostly on successful demonstrations and has little reason to predict the consequences of bad actions. We introduce FACT, a causal World-Action Model that predicts future video and task progress conditioned on the executed action.

This action-conditioned interface allows failure rollouts to supervise action consequences, turning bad actions into valid future targets rather than being discarded. Failure-aware training makes the progress predictor aware of both successful and failed action outcomes, which can optionally be used to score sampled action candidates at inference.

Extensive experiments on simulation and real-world bimanual manipulation tasks show that FACT outperforms many existing baselines, improves as failure data are incorporated into training, and reduces success-biased future hallucination under bad actions. See more details at https://fact-wam.github.io/

summary.en: The paper introduces FACT, a causal world-action model that predicts future video and task progress conditioned on the executed action. The authors argue that models trained mostly on successful demonstrations have little reason to predict bad-action consequences. FACT uses failure rollouts as valid future targets, training its progress predictor on both successful and failed outcomes; at inference, the predictor can optionally score candidate actions. Experiments on simulated and real-world bimanual manipulation tasks report that FACT outperforms many existing baselines, improves with failure data, and reduces success-biased future hallucination under bad actions.
summary.zh: 论文提出 FACT，一种因果世界-动作模型，根据已执行动作预测未来视频和任务进展。作者指出，许多此类模型主要用成功示范训练，因此较少预测不良动作的后果。FACT 将失败轨迹作为有效的未来预测目标，使进展预测器同时学习成功与失败结果；推理时还可用它为候选动作评分。仿真和真实世界双臂操作任务实验显示，FACT 优于多种现有基线，纳入失败数据后表现提升，并减少了不良动作下偏向成功的未来幻觉。

items.title: FACT: Failure-Aware Causal Training for World-Action Models

sections.text:
Gaze coordinates attention in human interaction through coupled eye, head, and eyelid motion. A humanoid robot must choose where to look while generating a suitable movement toward that target; fixed tracking rules alone do not model the temporal structure of human gaze.

We separate these tasks with an asynchronous vision-language model that selects a scene referent, a reactive perception module that maintains fixation, and a Realistic Gaze Transformer (RGT) that generates target-conditioned motion.

RGT is a Transformer-VAE trained on markerless human recordings retargeted to the robot's 11-DoF joint space: self-supervised pretraining encodes recent full-head history, and autoregressive fine-tuning exposes the model to its own predictions during rollout.

At inference, a four-dimensional binocular-eye trajectory conditions coordinated neck and eye motion; an auxiliary blink predictor triggers eyelid templates during playback.

On a two-second benchmark in which all controllers receive the same ground-truth target, RGT-Base obtains the lowest reported overall seven-joint MSE, and physical demonstrations show the integrated targeting and control pipeline.

The evidence establishes robot-space kinematic fidelity and real-time RGT inference; perceived naturalness and open-vocabulary target-selection accuracy remain questions for controlled evaluation.

summary.en: The paper separates robot gaze into scene-referent selection, fixation maintenance, and target-conditioned motion generation, and presents the Realistic Gaze Transformer (RGT) for coordinated eye and neck movement. RGT is a Transformer-VAE trained on markerless human recordings retargeted to the robot’s 11-DoF joint space, with self-supervised history encoding and autoregressive fine-tuning. A four-dimensional binocular trajectory conditions motion, while an auxiliary predictor triggers eyelid templates. On a two-second benchmark with shared ground-truth targets, RGT-Base reports the lowest overall seven-joint MSE. Physical demonstrations show the integrated pipeline; perceived naturalness and open-vocabulary target-selection accuracy remain unevaluated.
summary.zh: 论文将机器人注视分为场景目标选择、持续注视和目标条件运动生成，并提出 Realistic Gaze Transformer（RGT）生成协调的眼部与颈部动作。RGT 是在重定向至机器人11自由度关节空间的人体无标记记录上训练的 Transformer-VAE，先自监督编码近期全头部历史，再以自回归方式微调。推理时，双眼四维轨迹用于条件化颈眼运动，辅助眨眼预测器触发眼睑动作模板。在目标一致的两秒基准测试中，RGT-Base 的整体七关节均方误差最低；实体演示展示了集成管线。证据支持其运动学保真度和实时推理能力；自然度及开放词汇目标选择准确性仍待受控评估。

sections.text:
Ensuring safety of learning-enabled robotic manipulation across diverse embodiments and tasks still requires significant manual engineering. For collision avoidance, existing approaches typically rely on embodiment-specific learned safety approximations or simplified robot models together with stopping-based fallback controllers that compromise performance.

In this paper, we propose an embodiment-agnostic safeguarding approach, X-Safe, which provides formal probabilistic guarantees for collision avoidance without model simplifications or learned safety functions. By operating in the configuration space, our safeguarding method works with different types of robot policies.

X-Safe reasons locally around the current configuration to establish safe regions and uses action masking to restrict the policy's support to these safe regions. We demonstrate X-Safe on two embodiments and three policies, both in simulation and on hardware.

We observe less than half of the performance degradation compared to state-of-the-art safeguarding, and empirically corroborate our formal collision avoidance guarantees.

summary.en: The paper proposes X-Safe, a collision safeguarding method intended to work across robot embodiments and policies. It reasons about safe regions near the current configuration and masks actions so that a policy can select only actions within those regions, aiming to provide probabilistic collision-avoidance guarantees without simplified models or learned safety functions. The authors demonstrate the method in simulation and on hardware with two embodiments and three policies. They report less than half the performance degradation of state-of-the-art safeguarding and empirically corroborate the formal guarantees.
summary.zh: 论文提出 X-Safe，一种面向不同机器人本体与操作策略的碰撞防护方法。它在构型空间围绕当前构型建立安全区域，并通过动作屏蔽将策略可选动作限制在这些区域内，旨在提供概率形式的碰撞避免保证，无需简化模型或学习安全函数。作者在两种机器人本体、三种策略的仿真和硬件实验中展示该方法，报告其性能下降不到现有最先进防护方法的一半，并以实验结果支持其形式化保证。

items.title: X-Safe: Embodiment-Agnostic Safeguarding for Robot Arm Manipulation Policies via Action Masking

sections.text:
Scaling embodied robot learning requires large and diverse manipulation datasets, but collecting real-world demonstrations remains expensive in human effort and robot time.

Simulation provides a scalable alternative, yet converting a real workspace into a robot-learning-ready environment still requires substantial manual effort for object extraction, asset processing, coordinate calibration, and trajectory specification.

We present AutoRSR, a highly automated real-to-sim-to real framework that converts scanned real-world workspaces into reusable embodied simulation assets and scalable manipulation data.

Given multi-view observations, robot states, and open-vocabulary semantic queries, AutoRSR reconstructs the workspace, extracts individual object assets, and automatically registers the reconstructed scene to the robot base frame at metric scale.

Starting from a small number of reference motions, AutoRSR then generates executable manipulation trajectories and scales them through trajectory interpolation and domain randomization. After workspace scanning and semantic queries, the remaining pipeline requires no manual object annotation, scene-to-robot calibration, or robot teleoperation.

Across three real-world manipulation tasks, policies trained on 1K automatically generated episodes per task achieve 73.3--86.7% real-world success rates, comparable to pi 0.5 trained from 150 human teleoperated demonstrations, while reducing the human time required for data generation by an order of magnitude.

These results demonstrate that real-world observations can be converted into metrically aligned, executable, and scalable simulation data with substantially reduced human effort.

summary.en: AutoRSR converts scanned real workspaces into reusable simulation assets and manipulation data. Using multiview observations, robot states, and open-vocabulary semantic queries, it reconstructs scenes, extracts object assets, and registers scenes to the robot base frame. From a small set of reference motions, it generates executable trajectories and scales them through interpolation and domain randomization. The authors report that, after scanning and querying, the pipeline needs no manual object annotation, scene calibration, or teleoperation. Across three real-world tasks, policies trained on 1,000 generated episodes per task reached 73.3–86.7% success, comparable to pi 0.5 trained on 150 human demonstrations, with an order-of-magnitude reduction in human data-generation time.
summary.zh: 论文提出 AutoRSR，将真实工作空间扫描结果转为可复用的仿真资产和操作数据。系统利用多视角观测、机器人状态及开放词汇语义查询重建场景、提取物体资产，并将场景注册到机器人基座坐标系；从少量参考动作出发生成并扩展可执行轨迹。作者称，除扫描和语义查询外，后续流程无需人工标注物体、场景校准或机器人遥操作。在三项真实操作任务中，每项用自动生成的1000条 episode 训练的策略成功率为73.3%至86.7%，与使用150次人工遥操作示范训练的 pi 0.5 相当，数据生成所需人工时间减少一个数量级。

sections.text:
Progress toward general intelligence in the physical world requires scaling robot learning across diverse environments and interactions. However, existing robot policies use shared parameters that remain fixed across interaction contexts.

When different operations favor competing parameter adjustments, fitting their mixture can leave individual operations insufficiently adapted. Our atomic-task diagnostics reveal competing update directions in both vision-language and action parameters, with source-improving updates increasing loss on other tasks.

This motivates MorphAct, a contextual parameterization framework that dynamically adjusts robot policy parameters as interaction contexts change. Two coupled generators produce context-dependent low-rank updates for the vision-language and action modules.

Learning and executing long-horizon robot manipulation as complete task trajectories raises data-collection costs, lim?its capability reuse, and causes local failures to cascade into later task stages.

We introduce manipulation units (MUs) as reusable operations, each defined by a local goal, an initi?ation condition, and observable success and failure criteria. MUs are learned and verified individually. During execution, consecutive MUs remain coupled through shared environ?ment dynamics.

We formulate MU-Structured Manipulation (MUSM) and realize it through MU-Centric Orchestration (MUCO).Given language and vision, MUCO constructs an MU sequence, matches each MU to compatible policy models in a frozen capability registry, and dispatches the model with the highest calibrated success rate.

Visual verification checks MU outcomes against success and failure criteria and governs transitions, enabling retry or fallback to another model from the current state without re-executing verified MUs. Canonical keys enable checkpoint reuse for equivalent MUs across tasks without new demonstrations or updates.

We evaluate MUCO on RLBench, RoboTwin 2.0, and five real-world tasks. MUCO achieves higher complete-task success and verified progress, stronger failure containment, and lower error propagation than baselines.

Results demonstrate cross-task MU reuse and het?erogeneous policy composition without joint training, shared backbones, or common action representations.

summary.en: The paper presents MUCO, which organizes long-horizon robot manipulation into reusable units with local goals, initiation conditions, and observable success and failure criteria. Given language and vision, it builds a unit sequence, selects policies from a capability registry, and uses visual verification to govern transitions, retries, or fallback. Evaluations on RLBench, RoboTwin 2.0, and five real-world tasks report improved complete-task success, verified progress, and failure containment over baselines, alongside cross-task reuse and heterogeneous policy composition without joint training.

sections.text:
Reinforcement-learning policies for robot locomotion can fail at deployment when operating conditions shift (e.g., rough or slippery terrain, payload changes, sensing degradation), and retraining or manual recalibration is often infeasible under on-device latency and memory constraints.

We study test-time adaptation (TTA) for robotic control: adapting a pretrained policy online and in a self-supervised manner during execution, without access to rewards. Our starting point is a lightweight baseline that updates only the actor using a frozen pretrained critic as a deployment-time performance surrogate.

Building on this, we introduce TEMPO, a test-time entropy-regularized, memory-guided policy optimization method that stabilizes critic-driven updates under severe shift.

TEMPO combines (i) an entropy-promoting regularizer on the critic's predictive distribution to mitigate overconfident extrapolation, and (ii) a score-based memory, inspired by prioritized replay, that prioritizes low-value ("hard") observations and applies importance sampling to focus limited computation on the most informative deployment conditions.

Across Go1, Go2, and G1 in MuJoCo Playground under four representative shifts and multiple architectures, TEMPO yields consistent gains, reaching up to 80% improvement in a single-device setting.

We further validate on a physical Unitree Go2 with an added calf payload, where fully on-device adaptation improves performance over the non-adapted baseline across real-world episodes.

summary.en: The paper studies self-supervised online test-time adaptation of pretrained robot control policies without reward access. Its TEMPO method uses a frozen critic as a performance surrogate and combines entropy regularization of the critic's predictive distribution with score-based memory to stabilize updates under shifts and prioritize difficult observations. Simulations in MuJoCo Playground across Go1, Go2, and G1 report consistent gains across four shifts and multiple architectures, reaching up to 80% improvement in a single-device setting. The authors also report better performance than a non-adapted baseline on a physical Go2 with an added calf payload.
summary.zh: 论文研究机器人控制的测试时自适应：在执行中以自监督方式在线调整预训练策略，无需奖励信号。作者提出 TEMPO，利用冻结评论家提供性能代理，并结合对评论家预测分布的熵正则化和基于分数的记忆机制，稳定分布偏移下的更新并优先处理困难观测。在 MuJoCo Playground 的 Go1、Go2 和 G1 仿真中，多个架构与四类偏移测试显示一致提升，单设备设置最高改善 80%。作者还报告，在加装小腿负载的实体 Unitree Go2 上，设备端自适应优于未适应基线。

sections.text:
Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed as high-level planners for embodied agents, with an emerging strategy of scaling test-time compute to improve capability.

However, we observe that doing so increases latency, token usage, and FLOPs while yielding uneven, often diminishing gains in downstream success, limiting where embodied agents can be deployed.

We argue that choosing when and where to spend test-time compute is central to bringing frontier performance to the real world, and we can budget inference at the planning level.

We introduce DIRECT, a routing framework that uses multimodal scene context to allocate compute at each step of a closed-loop agent, selecting a planner for every subtask, improving the success--cost Pareto frontier over fixed model selection.

Across three dominant scaling axes, namely chain-of-thought depth, model size, and memory history, our experiments on VLABench and RoboMME show that test-time compute is not a uniform lever: different axes yield qualitatively distinct capability gains.

We validate these insights on a physical Franka arm in a DROID setup spanning zero-shot manipulation and long-horizon chaining, where our router matches or exceeds a stronger model's success rate at up to 65% lower average latency.

Ultimately, our results show that naively scaling test-time compute is wasteful, and DIRECT can provide frontier-level embodied planning at a fraction of the cost. Project page can be found at jadee-dao.github.io/direct/.

summary.en: The paper introduces DIRECT, a routing framework that uses multimodal scene context to select a planner for each subtask in a closed-loop embodied agent, allocating test-time compute step by step. The authors note that scaling compute raises latency, token use, and FLOPs, while downstream success gains can be uneven or diminish. Experiments on VLABench and RoboMME examine chain-of-thought depth, model size, and memory history, finding distinct capability effects. On a physical Franka arm in a DROID setup, the router matches or exceeds a stronger model's success rate at up to 65% lower average latency.
summary.zh: 论文提出 DIRECT，根据多模态场景上下文，在闭环具身智能体的每个步骤为子任务选择规划器，以分配测试时计算资源。作者指出，增加推理计算会提高延迟、词元用量和 FLOPs，成功率收益则不均且可能递减。VLABench 与 RoboMME 实验比较思维链深度、模型规模和记忆历史等扩展维度，发现它们带来的能力收益不同。在 DROID 设置下的实体 Franka 机械臂实验涵盖零样本操作与长时程任务串联；作者报告路由器以最高低 65% 的平均延迟达到或超过更强模型的成功率。

sections.text:
Computationally lightweight manipulation policies predict executable actions with low inference latency, but prediction errors can limit task success. Iterative generative policies can achieve higher task success rates, but repeated network evaluations increase inference latency.

Refining action proposals from computationally lightweight policies can combine these strengths, but the amount of refinement needed varies across states.

We introduce RAIN (Refine Actions If Needed), a framework that predicts action errors at different refinement levels to decide whether and how much to refine each executable proposal, before performing any refinement.

We train an ensemble to predict these errors by comparing action proposals and their refined versions with expert actions from offline demonstrations, without requiring explicit labels of refinement needs. Calibration balances uncertainty, computation, and temporal consistency. We evaluate RAIN on eight ManiSkill tasks and four real-robot tasks.

In simulation, our policy achieves 66.6% success, approaching the best evaluated diffusion-policy success rate with 5.71 times lower policy latency. On the real robot, success increases from 55.0% with Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) to 72.5%, with comparable average successful completion time.

Matched controls show that dynamic routing maintains the strongest observed fixed-refinement success level with 26.6% fewer refiner evaluations. Project page: https://rain-policy.github.io/.

summary.en: RAIN is a framework for refining robot manipulation actions only when needed. It predicts action errors at different refinement levels, then decides whether and how much to refine a proposal. An ensemble is trained by comparing proposals and refined actions with expert actions from offline demonstrations, without explicit labels for refinement needs; calibration balances uncertainty, computation, and temporal consistency. Across the reported evaluations, simulation success was 66.6% with 5.71 times lower policy latency than the best evaluated diffusion policy. Real-robot success rose from 55.0% with ACT to 72.5%, with comparable average completion time for successful tasks.
summary.zh: RAIN是一种按需细化机器人操作动作的框架，先预测不同细化程度下的动作误差，再决定是否以及细化多少，以减少轻量策略的预测错误，同时避免反复运行生成策略带来的延迟。作者用离线示范中的专家动作比较原始与细化提案，训练集成模型，无需显式标注细化需求，并通过校准平衡不确定性、计算量和时间一致性。仿真中报告成功率66.6%，策略延迟为最佳评估扩散策略的五分之一左右；真实机器人任务成功率从ACT的55.0%升至72.5%，成功完成时间均值相近。对照实验显示，动态路由在维持观测到的最强固定细化成功水平时，细化器调用减少26.6%。

sections.text:
Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong performance on local robot manipulation, yet their success does not readily translate to long-horizon mobile manipulation. In our experiments, a pretrained subtask VLA achieves 80% success rate on atomic manipulation tasks but only 19% when these skills are composed into mobile manipulation.

We argue that this gap stems from failures across the execution process rather than from local manipulation capability alone. To uncover these bottlenecks, we systematically diagnose failures in long-horizon mobile manipulation and identify three dominant regimes: task planning, navigation and base positioning, and local manipulation.

Based on this diagnosis, we develop failure-guided agentic intervention that augments a fixed subtask VLA with demonstration-based planning guidance, adaptive visual memory, accessibility-aware base adjustment, and local end-effector adjustment.

On RoboCasa365, these interventions progressively improve task success from 19% to 47%, with the finalized system reaching 49% on held-out episode seeds, compared with 18% for the baseline. The same design improves performance from 14% to 37% on BEHAVIOR-1K and from 5/20 to 13/20 on real-robot tasks.

These results suggest that reliable mobile manipulation can be advanced by diagnosing and intervening on the current bottleneck, rather than uniformly scaling the underlying policy. Our code will be released at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/Cracking-Mobile-Manipulation.git.

summary.en: The paper examines why vision-language-action models that perform well on local manipulation may fail on long-horizon mobile tasks. In the authors’ experiments, a pretrained subtask model reached 80% success on atomic tasks but 19% when skills were composed. They identify failures in planning, navigation and base positioning, and local manipulation, then add demonstration-based planning guidance, adaptive visual memory, accessibility-aware base adjustment, and end-effector adjustment. On RoboCasa365, success rose to 47%, with the final system reaching 49% on held-out episode seeds versus 18% for the baseline. The paper also reports gains on BEHAVIOR-1K and real-robot tasks.
summary.zh: 本文分析视觉语言动作模型用于长时程移动操作时的失败，指出局部操作能力并不能直接转化为组合任务成功。实验中，预训练子任务模型在原子操作上的成功率为80%，组合成移动操作后为19%；作者将瓶颈归为任务规划、导航与底盘定位、局部操作三类。针对这些问题，系统加入基于示范的规划指导、自适应视觉记忆、考虑可达性的底盘调整和末端执行器调整。在RoboCasa365上，干预使成功率由19%逐步升至47%，最终系统在留出种子上为49%，基线为18%；BEHAVIOR-1K和真实机器人任务也有提升。作者据此认为，诊断并处理当前瓶颈有助于提升可靠性。

sections.text:
Although recent years have seen significant progress of humanoid robots in walking and running, the frequent foot strikes with ground during these locomotion gaits inevitably generate high instantaneous impact forces, which leads to exacerbated joint wear and poor energy utilization.

Roller skating, as a sport with substantial biomechanical value, can achieve fast and continuous sliding through rational utilization of body inertia, featuring minimal kinetic energy loss. Therefore, this study proposes a novel humanoid robot with each foot equipped with a row of four passive wheels for roller skating.

A deep reinforcement learning control framework is also developed for the swizzle gait with the reward function design based on the intrinsic characteristics of roller skating.

The learned policy is first analyzed in simulation and then deployed on the physical robot to demonstrate the smoothness and efficiency of the swizzle gait over traditional bipedal walking gait in terms of Impact Intensity and Cost of Transport during locomotion.

A reduction of $75.86\%$ and $63.34\%$ of these two metrics indicate roller skating as a superior locomotion mode for enhanced energy efficiency and joint longevity.

summary.en: The study proposes a humanoid robot fitted with four passive wheels on each foot and develops a deep reinforcement learning framework to control a swizzle skating gait. Its reward design reflects characteristics of roller skating, which the authors describe as using body inertia for continuous sliding with less kinetic energy loss. The learned policy is analyzed in simulation and then deployed on a physical robot. The abstract reports smoother, more efficient swizzle locomotion than traditional bipedal walking in terms of impact intensity and cost of transport, with reductions of 75.86% and 63.34%, respectively. The authors suggest skating may improve energy efficiency and joint longevity.
summary.zh: 本文提出一种每只脚装有四个被动轮的双足人形机器人，并开发基于深度强化学习的滑行交叉步控制框架。作者将轮滑描述为利用身体惯性实现连续滑行、减少动能损失的运动方式，并依据其特点设计奖励函数。学习到的策略先在仿真中分析，再部署到实体机器人上。摘要称，与传统双足行走相比，交叉步滑行在运动冲击强度和运输成本方面表现更平顺、高效；这两项指标分别降低75.86%和63.34%。作者据此认为轮滑可能提升能效并延长关节寿命。

sections.text:
Dynamical system (DS)-based learning from demonstration generates flexible robot motions, but existing guarantees rely on certificate generation to obtain formal guarantees of safety and goal convergence.

We propose a symbolic supervisory control architecture that automatically generates a fail-safe backup plan, certifying safety, reachability, and actuator feasibility directly from the robot's dynamics, independent of the learned DS.

A nominal controller tracks the learned DS, while the supervisory controller monitors safety and target convergence, providing non-conservative intervention when the nominal controller violates necessary constraints.

Experimental results include simulations and real robot deployment with various 2D and 3D datasets, including handwriting datasets, validating the effectiveness of our approach in providing formal guarantees with learned motion even in complex, dynamic environments.

summary.en: The paper proposes a symbolic supervisory control architecture that generates a fail-safe backup plan for motions learned from demonstrations. Based directly on robot dynamics and independently of the learned dynamical system, it certifies safety, reachability, and actuator feasibility. A nominal controller tracks the learned motion, while a supervisor monitors safety and target convergence and intervenes when necessary constraints are violated. The authors report simulations and real-robot deployment across 2D and 3D datasets, including handwriting, as evidence of effectiveness in complex, dynamic environments.

Technologies, such as co-simulation, in particular, digital twins (DTs) are used for comprehensive and reliable prototyping, verification and validation (V&V) of control systems. Feedback loops spanning simulations and physical setups allow different forms of experimentation with robots and autonomous systems, but handling multiple realities calls for more specific support from control-engineering modeling techniques. The authors propose a framework for mixing or separating control inputs and feedback signals, including stimuli and responses, across plants operated simultaneously in multiple realities. sections.text:
Many robotic tasks, such as inverse kinematics, motion planning, and contact-rich manipulation, can be formulated as optimization problems.

Solving these problems requires addressing inherent nonlinear kinematics, complex contact dynamics, long-horizon correlations, and multi-modal optimization landscapes, each posing distinct challenges for state-of-the-art optimizers.

While existing methods tackle these issues through problem-specific strategies, such specialization inherently limits cross-task generalization, requires heavy engineering effort in problem reformulation, and hinders multi-task autonomy.

Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) offers a compelling framework that generalizes across diverse robotic tasks via strategic exploration of the solution space. However, it typically suffers from combinatorial complexity when applied naively, resulting in slow convergence and excessive storage space in high-dimensional domains.

To address this limitation, we propose Tensor Train Tree Search (TTTS), which leverages tensor factorization to exploit implicit correlations among different branches within the decision tree.

By utilizing the resulting compact, linear-complexity representation, TTTS significantly reduces both computation and storage overhead, thereby enabling highly efficient global decision making.

Experimental results across inverse kinematics, motion planning around obstacles, legged robot manipulation, multi-stage motion planning, and bimanual whole-body manipulation demonstrate the efficiency of TTTS for generalized robot optimization over a diverse set of tasks.

summary.en: The paper presents Tensor Train Tree Search (TTTS), which applies tensor factorization to Monte Carlo Tree Search to capture implicit correlations among decision-tree branches. The authors say its compact, linear-complexity representation reduces computation and storage overhead for global decision making. They report experiments on inverse kinematics, obstacle-avoiding motion planning, legged robot manipulation, multi-stage planning, and bimanual whole-body manipulation, describing the results as demonstrating efficiency across diverse robot optimization tasks.

sections.text:
Humanoid Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) can execute impressive motions, but downstream applications such as loco-manipulation demand high whole-body positional accuracy. Existing BFMs suffer from a systematic command-execution gap, where executed motions deviate from desired ones.

We show that additional test-time compute can improve execution without retraining the BFM. First, we introduce Test-Time Command Optimization (TTCO), which adapts the input command to the specific BFM to produce an executed trajectory closer to the desired motion.

TTCO finds such commands by sampling-based optimization through closed-loop simulations of the BFM and robot dynamics. Across three BFMs on the AMASS dataset, TTCO reduces mean global body-position error by 79-84% in simulation.

Second, we analyze test-time compute scaling and derive an approximate compute-optimal strategy that can sustain performance gains as the compute budget increases. Third, TTCO can generate BFM-specific action labels from recorded robot trajectories without requiring the original teleoperation body-motion commands.

Simulation and real-robot experiments show that these labels are effective for training high-level loco-manipulation policies. This method also supports reusing existing demonstrations across BFMs.

summary.en: The paper addresses the gap between desired and executed motions in humanoid Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs), proposing test-time compute to improve accuracy without retraining. Test-Time Command Optimization (TTCO) adapts commands through sampling-based optimization in closed-loop simulations of the BFM and robot dynamics. In simulation across three BFMs on AMASS, the authors report a 79–84% reduction in mean global body-position error. They also analyze compute scaling and report that labels derived from recorded robot trajectories work for training high-level loco-manipulation policies in simulation and real-robot experiments.

Robot policies map observations to actions, typically using multilayer perceptrons (MLPs).Yet robot dynamics and control objectives involve multiplicative interactions among observable physical variables. MLPs can approximate these interactions but must learn them implicitly, at a representational cost.

We introduce PRISM (Polynomial Representations for Interaction-Structured Motor Control), a physics-motivated yet data-driven representation that learns multiplicative interactions by recursively adding scaled bilinear features, without enumerating all polynomial terms.

Replacing only the MLP's first affine layer, PRISM is plug-and-play for reinforcement and imitation learning, requiring no changes to training objectives, sensing, or controllers. Across humanoid locomotion and contact-rich manipulation, PRISM improves survival from 51.0\% to 92.5\%, outperforming even larger MLPs.

More strikingly, its performance advantage persists under out-of-distribution changes in friction, robot mass, and payload, without retraining.

PRISM also exhibits sensorless compliance-like behavior, increases failure-recovery success from 40.9\% to 52.3\% without explicit admittance control, improves real-robot manipulation, and learns features that better predict physical quantities. These results make PRISM a compelling alternative to standard MLPs for robot policy learning.

The project page is available at https://lsh3163.github.io/prism/.

summary.en: The paper introduces PRISM, a physics-motivated, data-driven representation that learns multiplicative interactions by recursively adding scaled bilinear features without enumerating all polynomial terms. It replaces only an MLP’s first affine layer and is presented for reinforcement and imitation learning. The authors report gains in humanoid locomotion, contact-rich manipulation, and real-robot manipulation, as well as advantages under changes in friction, robot mass, and payload without retraining. These claims are limited to the tasks and evaluations described in the abstract.

Human demonstrations provide strong priors for robot manipulation, yet it is non-trivial to transfer them to execute on real robots due to the kinematic gap.

In dexterous manipulation, it remains challenging to track long-horizon, contact-rich sequences even in simulators: a reference-tracking policy must keep objects on their target trajectories while preserving demonstrated joint motion and contact timing.

Existing approaches often rely on hand-crafted reward tuning that require per-sequence tuning and break under limited interaction budgets. We introduce ConTrack, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework that scales with tracking data.

ConTrack treats object tracking as a constraint and allocates remaining control authority to motion fidelity, which allows it to adapt task--style trade-offs online using a dual-variable update. In addition, ConTrack also stabilizes long-horizon learning with an adaptive mid-trajectory reset library that reuses policy-reachable simulator states.

Our qualitative and quantitative results in simulation tracking and real robot demonstrate that ConTrack improves success and object pose accuracy significantly over prior arts while preserving joint and contact fidelity. Website: https://www.lyt0112.com/projects/ConTrack.

It treats object trajectory tracking as a constraint and allocates remaining control authority to motion fidelity, adapting the task-style trade-off online with a dual-variable update. An adaptive mid-trajectory reset library reuses policy-reachable simulator states. The authors report improved success and object-pose accuracy over prior methods in simulation tracking and real-robot evaluations, while preserving joint-motion and contact fidelity.

Transferring human demonstrations to dexterous robots remains challenging because differences in hand morphology and contact dynamics often cause retargeted motions to fail at producing the intended object behavior. We present \textbf{FoLD}, a framework for learning dexterous manipulation of articulated objects through explicit force guidance.

FoLD compute compensatory force fields from human demonstrations together with the robot's current interaction state, yielding a force prior that promotes the demonstrated object motion. This force prior informs a residual policy that adapts retargeted hand motions to the contact requirements of the task.

We evaluate FoLD on a public benchmark for articulated object manipulation, where it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across tasks and embodiments. We further validate FoLD on real dexterous robot platforms, demonstrating successful transfer of human manipulation skills to robot execution.

Here is the link of our project page: https://gghgghgghgg.github.io/FoLD-project-page/.

sections.text:
Navigation for humanoid robots is critical, yet large-scale evaluation on physical hardware is often impractical due to cost and safety concerns, making simulation benchmarks essential.

Existing VLN benchmarks achieve physically executable navigation, but still assume （1） all hazards are observable from elevation maps; （2） realized motions closely match desired motions.

In real environments, however, fallen bottles may be ambiguous in elevation maps, while phones and water spills may be difficult to differentiate; hazard avoidance by the locomotion policy can cause the robot's actual trajectory to deviate from the path intended by the VLN policy.

Such command-execution mismatch can accumulate and lead the robot toward unintended locations. To expose these failure modes, we introduce a benchmark that models both elevation-subtle hazards and execution deviations, together with a closed-loop VLN + locomotion control framework that continuously realigns high-level navigation with the robot's actual state.

We evaluate navigation in simulation and further validate the locomotion policy on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid robot. Results show that semantic input reduces contact with hazards poorly represented in elevation maps, while anti-deviation improves navigation success.

These findings highlight the need to evaluate humanoid navigation jointly in terms of route completion and hazard avoidance.

items.title: What the Elevation Map Cannot See: Semantic-Aware Locomotion and Execution-Aware Navigation for Humanoid Robot

Contact-rich manipulation requires robots to coordinate not only where to move, but also how contact and force should evolve throughout an interaction.

Yet most robot policies represent actions primarily as motion trajectories, using tactile signals as inputs or auxiliary prediction targets without explicitly encoding contact dynamics in the action representation.

We propose ILA (Interaction Latents as Actions), which uses decodable interaction latents that jointly capture the evolution of motion, contact, and force application as policy action units, providing a shared representation for action generation, evaluation, and offline improvement.

We learn these latents through visually conditioned joint action-tactile reconstruction with a time-conditioned implicit decoder. Using them as flow-matching generation targets supports post-training of pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world action models (WAMs), as well as training flow-matching policies from scratch.

A shared decoder maps generated latents to executable actions. For offline improvement, we learn a tactile-conditioned expert reference model from interaction latents encoded from expert demonstrations.

The resulting expert-consistency rewards guide weighted learning from successful rollouts, while observation-compatible expert references guide correction of low-reward predictions from failed rollouts.

Across three policy families, ILA improves success rates averaged over four real-world tasks by 21.0-36.5 percentage points relative to tactile-conditioned direct-action baselines. Ablations highlight the benefit of encoding contact evolution in action targets beyond tactile conditioning, while the same latent space supports expert-guided offline improvement.

Project website: https://mrsecant.github.io/ILA/.

We present TacClaw-Infinity, a large-scale structured Vision-Tactile-Language-Action (VTLA) dataset for contact-rich manipulation, collected with TacClaw, a tactile-enabled UMI-style handheld interface that records synchronized visual observations, fingertip tactile signals, and end-effector trajectories without requiring a target robot during data collection.

Offline navigation demonstrations are multimodal, because one observation often allows several valid actions, such as passing an obstacle on either side. Behavior cloning averages these actions, potentially leading to unsafe routes.

Multimodal policies must discover the alternatives from the data, but similar states can lead to different routes whose current actions overlap. In navigation, the alternatives have a geometric cause and can be computed from one observation.

We propose a hierarchical neural-network policy that computes candidate modes from local geometry and learns from demonstrations which mode to follow and how. A high-level policy selects a mode using the goal and its previous choice among a set of candidate modes, and a low-level policy turns it into an action.

In simulation, the policy succeeds in over 95\% of seen and unseen test cases, compared with at most 43\% and 20\% for four offline learning baselines and 79\% and 67\% for a heuristic that uses the same modes without learning. The simulation-trained policy also transfers to a LimX Tron 1 bipedal robot.

While multi-fingered dexterous robot hands have the potential to provide human-level dexterity, using them for functional manipulation remains difficult because task success depends on precise contact, coordinated arm-hand motion, and reactive recovery from execution errors.

Precise contact depends on complex contact dynamics that are difficult to model accurately in simulation, motivating real-world learning. However, real-world demonstrations in the full arm-hand control space are costly and noisy because each trajectory must coordinate arm motion with high-DoF multi-finger contact.

Small execution deviations can further cause slipped contact or premature force application, making recovery from off-nominal contact states important for robust execution. To deal with these challenges, we propose HiFun, a hierarchical real-world RL framework for functional dexterous manipulation tasks.

Our key insight is to decouple the control complexity into a functional hand skill for precise contact execution and an arm-hand coordination policy for arm control and hand-skill activation.

This design enables effective real-time human intervention for reactive recovery learning and efficient data collection with Dynamic Movement Primitive (DMP) augmentation. Across six real-world tasks on two dexterous hands, HiFun achieves 98.3% average success within one hour of online training and remains robust to dynamic disturbances.

The project page is available at https://hly-123.github.io/HiFun/.

items.title: HiFun: a Hierarchical Framework for Efficient Functional Dexterous Manipulation Learning

Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly incorporate intermediate reasoning to improve robotic manipulation, yet existing approaches primarily reason about observed states without explicitly anticipating future scene evolution.

Extending such reasoning to explicit future rollouts at every inference step, however, introduces substantial computational overhead. We propose IG-VLA, a VLA reasoning framework that enables models to imagine the future and internalize the gist.

Our Latent Spatiotemporal Reasoning learns to imagine task-relevant future scene evolution directly in visual representation space, guiding action prediction without costly pixel-level video generation.

To further reduce inference overhead, we introduce Scene Gist Memory, which internalizes reasoning-derived scene-behavior associations into a compact Scene Gist Token, preserving the benefits of future reasoning while bypassing explicit future imagination at inference.

Extensive experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and VLABench demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of IG-VLA. On the LIBERO-Plus Language suite, both the reasoning and gist policies outperform the strongest baseline by nearly 6% in success rate.

The gist policy also achieves up to 6.38x speedup over baselines, reducing inference latency from 1081ms to 169.5ms per action chunk on a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU. These results demonstrate that future spatiotemporal reasoning can be effectively internalized for efficient VLA deployment.

items.title: Imagine the Future, Internalize the Gist: Efficient VLA Reasoning via Internalized Spatiotemporal Imagination

We present FoveaVLA, a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model that replaces the wrist camera with learned foveation actions. Wrist cameras provide close-up detail but restrict the view to the end-effector's surroundings. External cameras see the whole scene, but the policy receives them at low resolution, so the fine detail needed for manipulation is lost.

FoveaVLA recovers this detail by predicting, alongside each action chunk, the interaction region to observe at the next policy query. The policy then receives crops of these regions, taken from the original-resolution images, together with the full views.

We build FoveaVLA on $\pi_{0.5}$ in two configurations, Single and Dual, using one or two external stereo cameras with full and foveal RGB and depth inputs, and post-train both on DROID with RoboInter interaction annotations.

Across four real-world task suites, FoveaVLA-Single achieves 70.8% success with one external RGB-D view, and FoveaVLA-Dual achieves 77.1%, versus 52.1% for the wrist-equipped $\pi_{0.5}$.Both match the baseline on plain pick-and-place and improve success with distractors, cloth manipulation, and far-away objects.

Digital twins are increasingly used in robotics to simulate interactions, predict action outcomes, and support planning. However, constructing accurate digital twins requires precise estimates of physical properties such as mass, friction, and center of mass, which are often difficult to obtain in real-world environments.

We propose probabilistic digital twins, which represent uncertain physical properties as probability distributions rather than fixed values. By simulating actions across these distributions, the twin predicts a range of possible outcomes and their likelihoods.

These probabilistic simulations can guide both human and robot actions by identifying actions that are effective despite physical uncertainty. We demonstrate this framework through human-robot interaction scenarios, including interfaces that communicate simulated outcomes to users and robot planning strategies that explicitly account for uncertainty.

Human demonstrations offer a scalable alternative to costly robot data collection for dexterous manipulation, but most human datasets lack force measurements. Dexterous manipulation requires not only visual and proprioceptive understanding but also the ability to anticipate and regulate interaction forces.

To scale force-aware human-robot co-training, we introduce EgoForce, a large-scale human tactile dataset capturing force-rich manipulation experience, and combine it with robot demonstrations for pretraining. We present FACT, a robot foundation model that cascades from prospective visual planning to force-aware refinement for dexterous manipulation.

FACT comprises two jointly trained components. A Track-Guided Coarse Planner jointly predicts actions, future video, and visual tracks. Future video and visual tracks also provide a shared task representation that facilitates cross-embodiment knowledge transfer and coarse action generation.

Building on this coarse plan, a Force-Action Joint Refiner jointly predicts future force and refines the coarse action, allowing anticipated force and action to shape each other during refinement.

We evaluate the model on ten tasks requiring fine-grained coordination and force feedback, including tool use, musical instruments, and precision laboratory procedures. Using as few as 10 robot trajectories with 90 human trajectories for fine-tuning, FACT outperforms both baselines, with success-rate gains of up to 60 percentage points over T-Rex.

Ablations show that force supervision in human pretraining data is crucial for downstream robot performance after fine-tuning, while visual track prediction and training with future-force prediction improve dexterous execution.

Experiments varying the human-robot data ratio during fine-tuning further suggest that FACT learns from human demonstrations nearly as effectively as from robot demonstrations.

Object-goal navigation requires an embodied agent to explore an unfamiliar environment, identify a target object, navigate toward candidate instances, and reliably determine whether the observed object satisfies the mission goal. This work investigates this problem through a two-stage development process.

In Stage I, a fixed modular framework is used to examine combinations of exploration, object detection, and target validation methods. The results reveal clear trade-offs among navigation performance, validation reliability, execution time, and model-related cost, with no single fixed configuration remaining preferable across all evaluated conditions.

These observations motivate F2A-ObjectNav (Fixed-to-Adaptive Object-Goal Navigation), an adaptive agentic architecture in which a rule-based Supervisor coordinates specialized components for navigation and exploration, object detection, target validation, semantic guidance, and Mission Memory.

The architecture uses event-driven recovery, strategy revision, candidate management, and conditional semantic guidance while retaining lightweight execution during normal operation.

F2A-ObjectNav is evaluated over 25 episodes in each of AI2-THOR, RoboTHOR, and ProcTHOR, achieving success rate (SR) / success-weighted path length (SPL) values of 0.84/0.52, 0.40/0.22, and 0.44/0.37, respectively.

In addition to task-level metrics, architecture-specific behavioral metrics are used to characterize semantic-guidance usage, strategy switching, recovery activation, memory-supported behavior, and decision stability.

The results show different patterns of adaptive intervention across the three environments, with higher intervention frequencies observed in RoboTHOR and ProcTHOR than in AI2-THOR.

Executing a vision-language-action (VLA) policy involves deciding when to continue an attempt and when to intervene to improve its chances of success. We introduce ACRO, an Actor--Critic rollout orchestration layer that makes these decisions for a fixed VLA.

ACRO seeks interventions that offer a more promising continuation, are physically feasible, and leave sufficient time to complete the task. A Critic learned from policy rollouts estimates success prospects to decide when to intervene and select a re-entry target along the executed trajectory.

Trajectory Retraction shortcuts the visited path to return the robot to that target, where the same VLA resumes execution from a fresh observation. We evaluate ACRO with GR00T N1.7 and $\pi_{0.5}$ across SimplerEnv, RoboCasa, and real-robot manipulation.

Under the same physical execution budget, including all return motion, ACRO improves success by 10.4, 7.3, and 21.7 percentage points, respectively. It also completes additional tasks as the execution budget grows. These results show that controlling when and where a policy resumes can turn its existing capabilities into more successful task executions.

Simulated environments enable scalable training data generation for embodied agents, but more data does not necessarily provide what a particular agent needs to learn.

Existing environment-generation pipelines largely optimize generic properties such as realism, diversity, or task coverage, while different pretrained policies can fail for different environmental reasons.

We therefore introduce WEDGE, a framework for weakness-guided navigation learning in which the failure modes of a pretrained agent guide the generation of training environments at each adaptation round.

Given a pretrained policy, WEDGE uses an LLM to propose executable weakness features from contrasting successful and failed rollouts, automatically validates them on the diagnostic set, and selects the strongest validated weakness based on its success-rate gap. The validated weaknesses are then mapped to the environmental factors that control them.

WEDGE varies these factors to construct environments in the difficulty regimes where the policy struggles, producing targeted training experience for adaptation. Across three navigation agents with different adaptation mechanisms, we find that policies exhibit distinct weakness profiles and benefit from different training environments.

Iterative re-diagnosis further shows that dominant weaknesses can persist or shift as the policy improves, providing updated guidance for subsequent environment construction.

Together, these results show that policy failures are not only diagnostic signals, but actionable guidance for constructing training environments that target a policy's current weaknesses.

We present LidarVerse, a real-time unified LiDAR world model for sensor simulation across tasks and sensors.

Existing LiDAR simulators largely follow one of two complementary paradigms: reconstruction-based methods preserve the geometry of a captured scene but require lengthy per-scene optimization, whereas generative methods amortize learning across data but lack the consistency needed for long-horizon rollouts.

LidarVerse brings both paradigms into a single, unified conditional generative framework. A universal tokenizer maps LiDAR range sequences into a shared latent space, where a bidirectional teacher learns a common interface for conditioning on a LiDAR prefix, an HD-Map, a persistent spatial cache, and optionally, text.

Varying the available scene evidence turns the same model into a generator of new worlds, a point-cloud forecaster, or a generalizable resimulator of observed scenes without per-scene optimization.

We distill the teacher into a four-step autoregressive causal student and maintain both a rolling temporal K/V cache and a world-aligned spatial cache, enabling persistent long-horizon rollouts with real-time inference at 11 FPS on a single H100 GPU.

LidarVerse achieves state-of-the-art performance on most reported metrics across all three evaluation protocols, while its tokenizer supports 32-, 64-, and 128-beam LiDAR and generalizes to an unseen scanning pattern.

These results demonstrate that generative and reconstruction-grounded LiDAR simulation can be realized within one model, providing the core capabilities for future closed-loop sensor simulation.

Embodied visual tracking requires a robot to identify a designated target from visual observations and control its own motion to follow that target through an environment. Following an isolated person is a comparatively simple demonstration of embodied visual tracking, but following the intended person among distractors remains challenging.

Existing methods exhibit a substantial drop in success from single-target to distractor tracking, motivating a focus on the shared spaces that person-following robots must navigate.

We present \method{}, a vision--language waypoint policy built around the hypothesis that visual and language representations should be aligned before tracking-specific motion is learned. The policy combines complementary frozen visual encoders, multiscale temporal context, a transformer backbone, and a lightweight head for robot-centric waypoint prediction.

Its training progresses through vision--language alignment, multimodal reasoning mid-training, and tracking specialization on 19,532 oracle episodes. Compared with 41.54\% distractor-tracking success for our earlier OmTrackVLA model, the complete multi-stage recipe achieves 55.80\%.

We then explore on-policy refinement using filtered oracle labels for states visited by the policy. This preliminary study adds 2.42 percentage points of distractor-tracking success, reaching 58.22\%, while reducing collision rate by 1.99 pts. The final policy records the highest distractor- and ambiguous-tracking success rates among the compared methods.

These results support staged multimodal learning as a promising direction for tracking among distractors and motivate further study of on-policy refinement for person following in shared spaces.

Robotic systems that must acquire information about a specific target often face severe occlusion from sur- rounding structures or from the target itself, such that a single camera viewpoint provides only partial information. Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a promising paradigm for scalable robotic manipulation, yet their reliance on success-only behavioral cloning leaves them brittle; lacking corrective training signals, minor execution errors rapidly compound into unrecoverable, out-of-distribution failures.

To address this limitation, we propose Adaptive Failure-Informed Learning (AFIL), an end-to-end framework that leverages failure trajectories as adaptive negative guidance for diffusion- and flow-based VLA policies.

We present VGM-VS, a visual servoing method built on a pretrained feed-forward visual geometry model. Given the current view and a reference image captured at the target configuration, we estimate the relative camera pose with a visual geometry model and apply it iteratively as the pose increment of a closed-loop pose-based visual servoing (PBVS) scheme.

The geometry-aware representation acquired from large-scale pretraining keeps this estimate reliable when the target is occluded, weakly textured, or covers only a small part of the image.

However, the scale ambiguity inherent to these models leaves the predicted translation defined up to an unknown scale, while the pose increment must be metric for robot control.

We close this gap with a scene-specific metric adaptation: the robot autonomously records image--pose pairs along a predefined motion starting from the target pose, and we fine-tune the camera head on these data, jointly learning the hand--eye transform and thus removing the need for a dedicated calibration process.

We evaluate our method on three real-world assembly tasks with demanding tolerances: USB-C cable picking, cable insertion, and RAM insertion. Running in real time at 30Hz, VGM-VS converges to submillimeter terminal accuracy on the cable tasks, and reaches success rates of 90--100\% when the target is moved during servoing.

It converges in all trials under initial displacements of up to 30cm from the reference pose and with 50\% of the target object occluded, outperforming the compared visual servoing baselines.

Differential-algebraic equations (DAEs) arise in power networks, chemical processes, and multibody systems, where algebraic constraints encode physical conservation laws. The safety of such systems is critical, yet safe control is challenging because algebraic constraints restrict allowable state trajectories.

Control barrier functions (CBFs) provide computationally efficient safety filters for ordinary differential equation (ODE) systems. However, existing CBF methods are not directly applicable to DAEs due to potential conflicts between the CBF condition and the constraint manifold.

This paper introduces DAE-aware CBFs that incorporate the differential-algebraic structure through projected vector fields. We derive conditions that ensure forward invariance of safe sets while preserving algebraic constraints and extend the framework to higher-index DAEs.

A systematic verification framework is developed, establishing necessary and sufficient conditions for geometric correctness and feasibility of DAE-aware CBFs. For polynomial systems, sum-of-squares certificates are provided, while for nonpolynomial and neural network candidates, satisfiability modulo theories are used for falsification.

The approach is validated on wind turbine and flexible-link manipulator systems.

Perceptive bipedal locomotion over sparse terrain remains a difficult challenge: model-based methods are precise but brittle to uncertainty, while model-free methods are robust but struggle to discover the precise, constrained motions required for safety-critical locomotion where small errors can cause catastrophic failures.

We propose a model-assisted reinforcement learning (RL) framework that combines both perspectives in three steps: （1） generate a safe reference trajectory using simplified models; （2） train a privileged teacher policy guided by a control Lyapunov function (CLF) reward built around the safe reference trajectory; and （3） distill the teacher into a vision-based student policy.

We validate our approach in simulation and demonstrate successful deployment on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot navigating sparse footholds with lateral constraints.

Tiny robots have limited computation and memory, yet visual navigation systems often maintain more state than a task requires. We ask whether persistent memory can instead be shaped by the task. We present \textbf{RingNav}, a \(10.6\)k--parameter visual heading estimator that constrains its memory to the circular manifold \(S^1\).

Reduced-order models (ROMs) make model predictive control (MPC) of high-dimensional nonlinear systems tractable, but the resulting modeling error can lead to constraint violations on the real system.

We introduce CoRE-MPC, a robust MPC formulation that plans with a nonlinear ROM and guarantees recursive feasibility and constraint satisfaction for the full-order system.

It can be applied with a broad class of nonlinear model reduction techniques and the resulting MPC does not require evaluating the full-order model online, thus ensuring computational efficiency. The key insight is in how the ROM affects the dynamics of the prediction error.

We account for this with two error radii that are propagated alongside the ROM and provide a guaranteed bound on the prediction error.

The approach is validated in simulation on an 80-state oscillator chain, a Burgers equation, and a 9,768-state finite-element soft robot, where a two-state ROM with data-driven bounds keeps all 1,628 nodes clear of a wall at a median solve time below 1 ms for a 20 ms control period.

Across these examples, CoRE-MPC is 13 to 61 times faster than full-order robust MPC at only 27 to 35% higher closed-loop cost, whereas existing certified schemes are either infeasible or at least twice as conservative. Code: [released upon publication].

Human listeners can often identify the intended object several words before an instruction ends. Robots, however, are typically designed to wait until the speaker has finished before deciding how to act. We present EarlyCommit, an open-source tool that lets a robot commit to the intended object while the instruction is being spoken.

After every recognized word, a fine-tuned text encoder scores each object in the scene. The robot acts when the calibrated probability of the best object reaches a threshold tau set by the user, so 1 - tau is the accepted risk of choosing the wrong object. Otherwise, it waits or asks.

The tool includes a streaming speech front end, a scene and instruction generator with exact word-by-word ground truth, and scripts to train, calibrate, and evaluate.

On instructions containing words never seen in training, EarlyCommit commits correctly 1.6 to 2 times as often as keyword matching, is right at least 92 percent of the time when it commits at tau = 0.9, and needs 31 to 35 ms per word on consumer GPUs.

Robot actions vary in both extent and mode: how much change they produce and what kind of change they produce. A latent action space that reflects this structure may make it easier for downstream policies to map latent actions to robot actions.

However, existing latent action methods typically rely on visual reconstruction from observation pairs without explicitly encouraging such structure.

We introduce Polar Latent Actions with Radial structure (PoLAR), which imposes a radial-direction structure on latent actions, encouraging radius to encode transition extent and direction to retain transition mode.

We instantiate this structure in hyperbolic space, whose expanding volume with radius offers a natural fit for more diverse transition modes at larger extents.

Across in-task and large-scale pretraining settings, PoLAR improves downstream policy performance in simulation and real-world robot experiments, outperforming latent action baselines and strong pretrained VLAs. These results suggest that structuring latent actions by extent and mode helps transfer visual pretraining to robot policy learning.

Instruction-Conditioned Motion Control (ICMC) separates parameter specification, instruction generation, and code synthesis for language-driven robot control, making execution outcomes traceable to instructions and programs.

We compare one-shot generation with ICMC under o1 and o4-mini on cube pick-and-place and letter-reshaping tasks for a UR5e arm in MuJoCo.
